official_site.name: Illinois State Board of Elections (statewide) and Chicago Board of Election Commissioners (city of Chicago)

model_plain: You can vote three ways: early in person (through Monday, Nov. 2; any Chicago voter can use any Chicago site), by mail (anyone can ask for a ballot, no excuse needed, apply by Oct. 29), or at the polls on Tuesday, November 3. City of Chicago voters deal with the Chicago Board of Elections; suburban Cook County voters deal with the Cook County Clerk.

deadlines.rule: Regular registration (by mail, at a DMV, or with a deputy registrar) closed Tuesday, October 6, 2026, the 28th day before the election. This date has passed. You can still register in person during the grace period (next row). State Board of Elections 2026 calendar: 'October 6, 2026: Close of Voter Registration. Last day for regular registration or transfer of registration within the offices of the election authority' (10 ILCS 5/4-6, 5-5, 6-29).

Online registration at ova.elections.il.gov closes Sunday, October 18, 2026 at 11:59 PM, the 16th day before the election. State Board 2026 calendar: 'October 18, 2026: Close of Online Voter Registration for the General Election. Last day for voters to register to vote through the State Board of Elections website' (10 ILCS 5/1A-16.5). After that, it's in person only.

Grace period registration runs Wednesday, October 7 through Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. You register and vote at the same visit. In Chicago: at the Downtown Supersite (137 S. State St.), the Board office (69 W. Washington, 6th floor), or any of the 50 ward early voting sites from Oct. 19 through Nov. 2, and on Election Day at your precinct polling place or any of the 51 vote centers. Chicago Board of Elections: 'Same Day Registration is available at all Early Voting/Vote Center sites, including 51 sites on Election Day. You will need two forms of ID, one with your current address.' Statutory basis: 10 ILCS 5/4-50, 5-50, 6-100.

registration.same_day_notes: Yes. Illinois calls it grace period registration and it runs through 7:00 PM on Election Day. You must do it in person and vote right then; you can't register during the grace period and take a mail ballot home. Bring two forms of ID, at least one showing your current address (examples the Chicago Board and news guides list: Illinois driver's license or state ID, passport, student ID, utility bill, bank statement, lease or mortgage, paycheck, a piece of government mail). Chicago: any early voting site through Nov. 2, any of 51 vote centers on Nov. 3. Suburban Cook County and the collar counties run their own sites; check your county clerk. Chicago Board of Elections phone: 312-269-7900.
registration.still_possible_now: Yes, in person. Online registration ended Sunday, October 18. You can still register and vote on the spot at any early voting site through Monday, November 2, or at the polls on Tuesday, November 3. Bring two forms of ID, one with your current address.

mail_ballot.who_gets_one: Anyone who asks. Illinois has no-excuse vote by mail. You must apply (online through your election authority, by mail, or in person) unless you're already on the permanent vote-by-mail list, in which case a ballot is mailed to you automatically every election. Election authorities started mailing ballots Thursday, September 24, 2026 (State Board calendar: 'mailing and delivery of ballots does not begin until Thursday, September 24, 2026'). If you're on the permanent list and have moved, update your registration or your ballot goes to the old address.

request_deadline.rule: Applications by mail or online must be received by Thursday, October 29, 2026 (5:00 PM in Chicago). You can still apply in person at your election authority's office through Monday, November 2. State Board 2026 calendar: 'Last day for the election authority to receive, by mail, an application for a vote by mail ballot and mail that ballot to the voter. In-person applications are still accepted until November 2, 2026.' Chicago: chicagoelections.gov, 'Apply for a Vote By Mail ballot'. Suburban Cook: cookcountyclerkil.gov. If you apply this late, plan to return the ballot by hand; there isn't time for two mail trips.

return_deadline.time: 7:00 PM CT if returned by hand or drop box; if mailed, postmarked by Nov. 3 and received by Tuesday, Nov. 17

return_options: secure drop box: Chicago has them at all 50 ward sites on the Board's drop box list (https://chicagoelections.gov/voting/drop-boxes); suburban Cook and the collar counties have them at early voting sites and clerk offices.

hand it in at any early voting site in your election jurisdiction through Nov. 2. On Election Day in Chicago, use the drop box at any of the 50 ward sites, 6 AM to 7 PM, or return it in person at the Board office, 69 W. Washington, Suite 600, by 7:00 PM. Do not bring it to a precinct polling place: the Chicago Board says 'Precinct election judges cannot accept Vote By Mail ballots. Vote By Mail ballots returned at precinct polling places will not be processed.' Outside Chicago, ask your county clerk where ballots can be returned on Election Day.

mail (USPS): counts if postmarked by Election Day and received by Nov. 17 (10 ILCS 5/19-8; DeKalb County Clerk's official date sheet: 'Tuesday, November 17: Deadline for validating and counting provisional ballots and timely postmarked mail ballots received after Election Day'). But see the gotchas on postmarks.
have someone you trust deliver it (the person carrying it signs the affidavit on the envelope)
mail_ballot.postage: Chicago and suburban Cook County return envelopes are postage-paid. Elsewhere in Illinois most election authorities also prepay return postage; if your envelope doesn't say 'no postage necessary,' add a stamp. (Sourced from past-cycle practice and news guides; read your envelope.)
mail_ballot.signature_witness_rules: Sign the certification envelope. No witness or notary. A panel of three election judges compares your signature to the one on file. Date the certification: under 10 ILCS 5/19-8, if the postmark is missing or unreadable, the date you wrote on the certification can establish that you voted by Election Day.
mail_ballot.cure_process: If judges reject your ballot for a missing or mismatched signature, the election authority must notify you (by mail, and by email or phone if they have it) within 2 days, and you have until 14 days after the election, Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to fix it with a signed statement or new signature. Watch your mail and email after you return your ballot. Illinois Election Code 10 ILCS 5/19-8.
mail_ballot.mail_cutoff_advice: Skip the mail now. In Chicago, put your ballot in a drop box at any of the 50 ward sites through Monday, Nov 2 (Monday to Friday 9 AM to 6 PM, Saturday 9 AM to 5 PM, Sunday 10 AM to 4 PM), or on Nov 3 from 6 AM to 7 PM. Do not take it to your precinct polling place: precinct judges can't accept it. USPS says to ask a retail counter clerk for a manual postmark when handing over a ballot; it is free. A mailed ballot counts if it is postmarked by November 3 and arrives by November 17. Follow your own election authority's return instructions outside Chicago.

early_in_person.hours_note: CHICAGO (official, chicagoelections.gov): Downtown Voting Supersite, 137 S. State St., and the Chicago Board of Elections office, 69 W. Washington St., 6th floor, opened Thursday, Oct. 1. Hours Oct. 1 to 25: Mon to Fri 9 AM to 6 PM, Sat 9 AM to 5 PM, Sun 10 AM to 4 PM. Hours Oct. 26 to Nov. 2: Mon to Fri 9 AM to 7 PM, Sat 9 AM to 5 PM, Sun 10 AM to 4 PM. All 50 ward sites open Monday, Oct. 19 through Monday, Nov. 2: Mon to Fri 9 AM to 6 PM, Sat 9 AM to 5 PM, Sun 10 AM to 4 PM. Any Chicago voter can use any site. Three campus sites (Chicago State, NEIU, UChicago Reynolds Club) run Oct. 28 to 30, 10 AM to 5 PM. On Election Day the Supersite and all 50 ward sites are open 6 AM to 7 PM as vote centers for any Chicago voter; the 69 W. Washington office is NOT open for voting on Election Day. SUBURBAN COOK: early voting began Oct. 7 at some sites and most sites open Oct. 19; hours vary by site and week; see cookcountyclerkil.gov. COLLAR counties: most opened Sept. 24 at the clerk's office, with more sites Oct. 19; DuPage's 24 permanent sites run weekdays 8 AM to 7 PM and weekends 9 AM to 5 PM.

election_day.in_line_rule: If you are in line at 7:00 PM, stay in line. You get to vote. Chicago voters can vote at their home precinct OR at any of 51 vote centers (the Downtown Supersite at 137 S. State and all 50 ward sites), per the Chicago Board: 'Voters can choose whatever voting site is most convenient for them, including on Election Day.' Outside Chicago, go to your assigned precinct unless your county says otherwise.

accepted: Most voters: no ID needed. You sign in and election judges compare your signature to the one on file. Chicago Board: 'While identification is not required, it is helpful to bring it in case there is a question about the voter's registration, address, signature.'

First-time voters who registered by mail without providing an Illinois driver's license, state ID number, or Social Security digits must show one ID: a current photo ID, or a current utility bill, bank statement, paycheck, government check, or other government document with your name and address (federal HAVA rule).

Grace period (same-day) registration: two forms of ID, at least one showing your current address. Examples: Illinois driver's license or state ID, passport, student ID, utility bill, bank statement, lease or mortgage, paycheck, government mail.
If you requested a mail ballot and show up in person, bring the mail ballot and surrender it (see gotchas).
id_rules.no_id_option: If you're required to show ID and don't have it, you vote a provisional ballot and have 7 days after the election (through Tuesday, November 10) to bring ID or proof to the election authority so it counts. Provisional ballots are validated by Nov. 17. Suburban Cook County voters: the Cook County Clerk's provisional page also says ID must arrive 'by 7 p.m. the Thursday after Election Day' (November 5), so send it by then to be safe.

in_the_booth.phones_detail: No Illinois law bans phones in the polling place, and you may use yours to look at notes or a sample ballot. But do not photograph or show your marked ballot: 10 ILCS 5/29-9 makes it a Class 4 felony to knowingly mark or show a ballot so another person can see how you voted (the Sun-Times guide: ballot selfies 'are prohibited' and a Class 4 felony; sticker selfies are fine). Election judges can ask you to put the phone away if it slows the line or bothers other voters. Source: https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/ilcs/ilcs3.asp?ActID=170&ChapterID=3 and https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/how-to-vote-illinois-general
in_the_booth.phones_short: You can read your plan on your phone; don't photograph your marked ballot.
in_the_booth.notes_detail: Yes. Bring a printed cheat sheet, a marked-up sample ballot, or a voter guide. The Sun-Times guide: 'Voters may bring notes, sample ballots, and endorsements into the booth.' Injustice Watch's judicial guide is built to be printed and carried in. Just don't hand your notes to other voters or leave campaign material in the booth.
in_the_booth.apparel_rule: Campaigning (electioneering) is banned within 100 feet of the polling place entrance (10 ILCS 5/17-29). Wearing a campaign button or shirt while you vote is generally tolerated as long as you vote and leave, but election judges can ask you to cover it. Safer to leave the gear in the car. (Statutory rule; no 2026 Chicago-specific guidance found.)

gotchas.text: Online registration ended Sunday, October 18 at 11:59 PM. You can still register, but only in person, with two IDs, at an early voting site (through Nov. 2) or a polling place or vote center (Nov. 3). You vote in the same visit.
gotchas.short: You can still register in person with two IDs, and vote in the same visit.

gotchas.text: The postmark trap. A mailed ballot counts if it's postmarked by Nov. 3 and arrives by Nov. 17, and the Supreme Court upheld that kind of rule in June 2026. The problem is USPS: much mail no longer gets a postmark, and Illinois clerks have been warning all year that an unpostmarked late ballot can be tossed. Your backstop: date the certification on the envelope, because state law counts a late ballot with no postmark if that date is Election Day or earlier (10 ILCS 5/19-8). Skip the mail now, or get a hand-stamped postmark at the counter. In Chicago, use a drop box at any of the 50 ward sites through Nov. 2, or on Election Day, Nov. 3, from 6 AM to 7 PM. Don't hand a mail ballot to your precinct polling place: Chicago precinct judges can't accept it and it won't be processed.
gotchas.short: Date the envelope certification, and use a drop box instead of the mail now.

gotchas.text: Requested a mail ballot but want to vote in person? Surrender it to the election judges to vote a regular ballot. If you never received it, or the election office says it never received the ballot you mailed, state law allows an affidavit. If you received it but lost it and cannot surrender it, you can vote a provisional ballot. It counts after officials confirm you are eligible and your mail ballot was not counted. Vote only once.
gotchas.short: Surrender your mail ballot at the polls to vote a regular ballot.

gotchas.text: Judicial retention needs 60% yes, not 50%, and the Cook County ballot has 61 retention questions: 1 Appellate Court justice (Bertina E. Lampkin) and 60 Circuit Court judges. A blank vote neither helps nor hurts a judge. Use Injustice Watch's 'Check Your Judges' guide (2026retention.injusticewatch.org), which prints a take-along report, plus the Chicago Bar Association and ISBA ratings.
gotchas.short: Retention needs 60% yes, and a blank vote neither helps nor hurts a judge.

gotchas.text: Two election offices, not one. City of Chicago voters use the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners (chicagoelections.gov, 312-269-7900). Suburban Cook County voters (Evanston, Oak Park, Cicero, Skokie, etc.) use the Cook County Clerk (cookcountyclerkil.gov). Early voting sites, drop boxes, and mail-ballot applications are specific to your jurisdiction. Also: on Election Day the 69 W. Washington office is closed for voting; the Supersite at 137 S. State is open 6 AM to 7 PM.
gotchas.short: Chicago voters use chicagoelections.gov; suburban Cook voters use the Cook County Clerk.

situations.question: I moved to a new address in Illinois.
situations.short: Re-register and vote in one visit at an early voting site or polling place, with two IDs.
situations.answer: Moving means re-registering at your new address. Online registration ended October 18, so register in person through Election Day at an early voting site or polling place. Bring two IDs (one showing your new address) and register and vote in one visit.
steps: In Chicago, any early voting site (through Nov 2) or any of the 51 Election Day vote centers can do it. Suburban Cook voters: check the Cook County Clerk's sites.
Moved after Oct 4? You haven't lived at the new address 30 days yet, so ask the election judges about voting from your old address.

situations.question: I just moved to Illinois from another state.
situations.short: If you've lived here since Oct 4, register and vote in person with two IDs.
situations.answer: You can register if you've lived at your Illinois address for at least 30 days before the election (since October 4). Bring two IDs, register in person at an early voting site or on Election Day, and vote right then. Online registration ended October 18.
steps: Bring two IDs, at least one with your current Illinois address, such as a lease, utility bill or bank statement.
Moved away from Illinois for good? You'd vote in your new state instead.

situations.question: I'm not registered to vote.
situations.short: Register and vote in one visit at an early voting site or your polling place; bring two IDs.
situations.answer: Online registration closed October 18. You can still register and vote in the same visit at a grace-period or early voting site through November 2, or at your polling place on November 3. Bring the required proofs of identity and residence.
steps: Check whether you're already registered at ova.elections.il.gov.
In person, bring two IDs, one showing your current address.
Registering in person means voting in person that day; you can't take a mail ballot home.

situations.question: The lookup can’t find me.
situations.short: The lookup needs your name exactly as registered: try your last name with the hyphen, a space, and joined.
situations.answer: Illinois’s lookup asks for your name, birth date, ZIP and street. Its first-name box takes letters only, so leave out hyphens, apostrophes and middle names there.
steps: Try your last name with the hyphen, with a space instead, and run together, and leave out any middle name or suffix.
If you’ve moved, try the ZIP code where you were registered before.
Still nothing? Call your county election office. A failed search doesn’t mean you’re not registered; records can lag.

situations.question: I went to the wrong polling place.
situations.short: In Chicago, any of the 51 vote centers works; in suburban Cook, go to your assigned precinct.
situations.answer: In Chicago, you can vote at your home precinct or at any of the 51 vote centers (the Downtown Supersite and the 50 ward early voting sites), including on Election Day. In suburban Cook County, you must vote at your assigned precinct on Election Day.
steps: Ask the judges to look you up; they can tell you your correct precinct and address.
Go there instead of voting provisionally. A provisional ballot in the wrong precinct may not count, in whole or in part.
Suburban Cook: find your precinct in Your Voter Profile on the Cook County Clerk's site.

situations.question: My mail ballot never came, or I lost it.
situations.short: Vote in person instead: surrender it if you have it, or sign an affidavit if it never came.
situations.answer: You can vote in person instead. Surrender your mail ballot if you have it. If it never arrived, state law allows an affidavit. If you received it but lost it, ask your election office about a replacement or cancellation before voting early; on Election Day, ask the election judges for a provisional ballot if you cannot surrender it.
steps: Tell your election office. Chicago: 312-269-7967 or votebymail@chicagoelections.gov. Suburban Cook: the Cook County Clerk's mail voting unit, 312-603-0946 or mail.voting@cookcountyil.gov.

For early voting through November 2, ask the election office about replacing or canceling a lost ballot first. On November 3, go to your precinct or a designated Election Day vote center. If your ballot is torn, bring the remaining portion to surrender.

Received it but lost it? At your polling place on Election Day, state law entitles you to a provisional ballot. It counts after officials confirm you are eligible and your mail ballot was not counted.

situations.question: I made a mistake on my mail ballot.
situations.short: Bring the whole ballot to an early voting site or the polls, surrender it, and vote in person.
situations.answer: Bring the ballot to any early voting site before Election Day, or to your precinct or a vote center on Election Day, surrender it, and vote a new ballot in person.
steps: Bring the whole ballot with you, marked or not.
Chicago questions: 312-269-7967. Suburban Cook: contact the Cook County Clerk.

situations.question: I mailed my ballot but now want to vote in person.
situations.short: A mailed ballot is your vote; if you haven't sent it, surrender it at the polls and vote.
situations.answer: Once you've mailed it, plan on that being your vote, since you can only vote once. If you haven't sent it yet, bring it to an early voting site or the polls, surrender it, and vote in person.
steps: Chicago voters get an email with tracking info; check it to see where your ballot is.
Think the record saying you voted is wrong? You can vote a provisional ballot.

situations.question: I don't have an ID.
situations.short: Most voters don't need ID; judges compare your signature instead.
situations.answer: Most Illinois voters don't need ID; you sign in and judges compare your signature. ID is needed only if you're registering the same day (two IDs) or you're a first-time voter who registered by mail without an ID number.
steps: If you're required to show ID and don't have it, you vote a provisional ballot.
Then get a copy of your ID to your election office within 7 days. Suburban Cook voters: send it by Thursday, Nov 5 to be safe.

situations.question: My name changed since I registered.
situations.short: If you didn't move, you can still vote in person by filling out an affidavit at the polls.
situations.answer: If you changed your name but didn't move and didn't update your registration, you can still vote in person by filling out an affidavit at the polls. You can't vote by mail under the old record.
steps: Changing your name at a Secretary of State facility? Ask them to update your voter registration too.

situations.question: I'm a college student.
situations.short: Vote by mail from your home address (apply by Oct 29), or register at school in person with two IDs.
situations.answer: You can vote from your home address by mail, or register at your school address if you've lived there 30 days. Apply for a mail ballot online by Thursday, October 29, or register in person at school with two IDs.
steps: Chicago campus early voting sites (Chicago State, Northeastern Illinois, UChicago Reynolds Club) are open Oct 28 to 30, 10 AM to 5 PM, and offer same-day registration.
For same-day registration, bring two IDs; a student ID plus something with your current address works.
Mail ballots must be postmarked by Nov 3 and arrive by Nov 17.

situations.question: I'll be away on Election Day.
situations.short: Vote early through Nov 2, or apply for a mail ballot by Oct 29.
situations.answer: Vote early: Chicago's sites are open through Monday, November 2, and any Chicago voter can use any site. Or apply for a mail ballot by Thursday, October 29 (in person at your election office through November 2).
steps: Mail ballots must be postmarked by Nov 3 and arrive by Nov 17. Skip the mail now: use a drop box, or ask the post office counter for a hand postmark.
Date the certification on the envelope; it can count if the postmark is missing.
Suburban Cook: early voting sites and hours are on the Cook County Clerk's site.

situations.question: I'm in line when polls close.
situations.short: Stay in line: if you're in line at 7 PM, you get to vote.
situations.answer: Stay in line. If you're in line at 7 PM, you get to vote.
steps: Don't leave, even if the line is long.
If a court orders polls to stay open late, people who vote after 7 PM vote provisional ballots.

situations.question: They said my signature doesn't match.
situations.short: Follow the notice you get; you have until Tuesday, Nov 17 to show why your ballot should count.
situations.answer: You can fight it. Your election office must notify you within 2 days of rejecting your mail ballot, and you have until Tuesday, November 17 to show why it should count.
steps: Follow the notice; you can bring evidence, like a new signature and ID, to the election office.
A panel of three election judges makes the final call.
Watch your mail and email after you send your ballot.

situations.question: What's a provisional ballot?
situations.short: It's a full ballot set aside until the election office confirms you're registered and eligible.
situations.answer: It's a full ballot that's set aside when your registration can't be found or your eligibility is questioned at the polls. It's counted after Election Day if the election office confirms you're registered and eligible.
steps: You have 7 days after Election Day to send documents that prove you're eligible, like a photo ID or utility bill.
It counts fully only in your assigned precinct, so go there if the judges direct you.
If it doesn't count, your affidavit still registers you for next time.

situations.question: How do I check my ballot was counted?
situations.short: In Chicago you get a tracking email for your mail ballot; for a provisional ballot, ask your election office.
situations.answer: Chicago mail voters get an email with tracking info when the ballot is mailed; call 312-269-7967 with questions. Provisional ballot status is posted by the Chicago Board, and suburban Cook voters can look it up in Your Voter Profile starting two weeks after the election.
steps: Chicago provisional ballots: see the Board's Provisional Ballot Status page.
Suburban Cook: use Your Voter Profile on cookcountyclerkil.gov, or call (312) 603-0900.

judicial_review.how_judges_get_here: New judges run in partisan elections. After a term, a sitting judge usually seeks retention: a yes-or-no vote without an opponent.
judicial_review.who_reviews: The Alliance’s 13 bar groups share an investigation and interview, then rate independently. The Chicago Bar Association conducts its own review. These are lawyer associations, not a state job-review commission.
judicial_review.what_the_rating_means: Recommended or qualified means that bar group found the candidate fit for the office. Groups can disagree. Some give a negative rating when a candidate does not participate, so read the explanation.
judicial_review.what_it_doesnt_mean: A rating does not tell you how a judge will rule in your case. A negative rating can reflect nonparticipation; it does not automatically establish misconduct.
judicial_review.to_keep_a_judge: A judge needs at least 60 percent yes votes on the retention question to stay. Blank votes count neither yes nor no. New candidates instead compete for the most votes.
judicial_review.history: Illinois’s constitution sets the retention threshold at three-fifths, which is 60 percent. It is higher than a simple majority.

heads_up.text: In a yes-or-no retention vote, a judge needs at least 60 percent yes to stay. Only votes on that judge’s question count.
